reasoning:
ServiceNow is precisely the kind of enterprise that Phil Fisher spent his career hunting: a company with a durable, compounding growth engine, a management team that has invested aggressively in R&D while simultaneously expanding profitability, and a competitive moat built not from patents or raw scale alone but from deep workflow entrenchment inside some of the world's largest organizations. The 3-year revenue CAGR from 2022 to 2025 stands at 22.4%, with revenues growing from $7.2 billion to $13.3 billion. Analysts expect $16.2 billion in 2026, sustaining that same 22% growth trajectory. This is not a company growing by acquisition of revenue; it grows by deepening penetration within its existing customer base and expanding across workflow domains -- IT, HR, customer operations, legal, finance -- on a single integrated platform.

R&D as a percentage of revenue is the signature Fisher metric, and here ServiceNow passes with distinction while carrying one carefully considered watch item. The company invested $2.96 billion in research and development in fiscal 2025, representing 22.3% of total revenue. The comparable figures are 24.4% in 2022, 23.7% in 2023, and 23.2% in 2024. In Q1 2026 that figure dipped to 21.8%. In absolute dollars, R&D has grown from $1.77 billion in 2022 to $2.96 billion in 2025 -- a 67% increase over three years. The mild declining trend in R&D as a percentage of revenue, from 24.4% to 21.8%, warrants honest attention. The dollar growth rate of R&D has also decelerated, from 20.1% in FY2023 to 16.4% in FY2025. This is not alarming -- $2.96 billion annually directed at a single enterprise platform is a formidable commitment -- but I would prefer to see the percentage stabilize at 22-23% rather than drift further toward 20%. For now I classify the R&D trend as maintaining with a mild watch flag rather than cutting, and it does not alter my overall assessment.

Margin quality is where ServiceNow has demonstrated impressive discipline. GAAP operating margins have expanded in every year measured: 4.9% in 2022, 8.5% in 2023, 12.4% in 2024, and 13.7% in 2025. Gross margins have held steady in the 77.5% to 79.2% range. Free cash flow margin -- the cleanest profitability signal for a subscription software business -- has expanded from 30.0% in 2022 to 34.1% in 2025, with FCF reaching $4.53 billion last year. A business generating 34% FCF margins while compounding revenue at 22% annually is genuinely scarce and is worth owning at a premium.

I address the AI disruption question directly and with full candor on both sides, as it is central to assessing durability over the 3-to-5-year horizon I require.

On AI as OPPORTUNITY: Now Assist and ServiceNow's agentic AI layer are not cosmetic additions to the platform. They are architecturally embedded in the workflow orchestration engine that governs how enterprises process incidents, manage employee onboarding, coordinate procurement, and resolve customer cases. The strategic thesis is sound and potentially compounding: as AI agents proliferate across enterprise operations, they require orchestration, governance, audit trails, and policy enforcement at scale. ServiceNow is positioning itself as the coordination layer those agents must traverse rather than a casualty of them. The $2.96 billion R&D budget, if directed effectively at this agentic opportunity, should produce a product expansion cycle that could push average contract values measurably higher. Management's appointment of Amit Zavery as President and Chief Product Officer -- a Google Cloud and Oracle veteran with deep AI infrastructure experience -- signals deliberate preparation for this transition, not defensive hedging. This is the kind of bold management move that Fisher found encouraging.

On AI as THREAT: The credible threat is not immediate destruction of enterprise workflow demand but three distinct longer-horizon risks. First, sufficiently capable general-purpose AI agents could bypass structured workflow software entirely for routine tasks, resolving incidents and approvals through natural language without engaging a formalized workflow engine. Second, Microsoft Copilot for Service, Salesforce Agentforce, and Workday AI represent well-funded platforms attempting to commoditize ITSM and HCM workflows using AI as the wedge into ServiceNow's territory. Third, the deceleration in R&D dollar growth (16.4% in FY2025 versus 20.1% in FY2023) raises a legitimate question: is ServiceNow reinvesting aggressively enough relative to AI-native competitors? I regard all three threats as real but primarily acute for lighter ITSM point solutions rather than for a platform entrenched across IT, HR, legal, finance, security, and customer operations simultaneously within Fortune 500 enterprises.

Net verdict: AI is net positive for ServiceNow over my 3-to-5-year horizon. Workflow orchestration complexity increases with AI agent proliferation rather than decreasing. The more AI agents an enterprise deploys, the more it needs an authoritative governance and coordination layer. ServiceNow's platform breadth and its deferred revenue base (growing 78% over three years to over $8 billion) confirm customers are deepening, not retreating. The primary monitoring variable is whether Now Assist generates measurable average contract value expansion per customer over the next 4 to 6 quarters.

On management: William McDermott has led the company since 2019 and executed an enviable capital allocation record. FCF has compounded from approximately $2.2 billion in 2022 to $4.5 billion in 2025. Share buybacks have accelerated ($1.84 billion in FY2025 versus zero in 2022). Debt has been held steady at $2.4 billion against a cash position of $5.2 billion. Acquisitions have been bolt-on and disciplined. McDermott's tenure of approximately 7 years is solid; I would prefer a founder-operator combination, but the operational execution has been exemplary.

On valuation: A forward P/E of 20.3x on analyst consensus EPS of $5.03 is not demanding for a business growing at 22% with 34% FCF margins. EV/Sales of 6.3x on 2026 estimates and FCF yield of 4.3% against the current market cap provide tangible support. The forward PEG approximates 0.92, unusually attractive for a company of this quality. I note the SBC load -- $1.96 billion in FY2025 against $1.75 billion GAAP net income -- as a structural dilution risk that must be weighed. The $12 per share decline last week appears to be macro-driven multiple compression rather than any deterioration in the business fundamentals. I remain bullish with moderate-high conviction at the current valuation.

As AI agents proliferate across IT, HR, legal, customer operations, and procurement, enterprises need workflow governance, cross-agent coordination, policy enforcement, and audit trails -- exactly what the Now Platform provides. The $2.96 billion annual R&D investment (22.3% of revenue in FY2025) is directed at this agentic expansion. Deferred revenue growing 78% over 2022-2025 to over $8 billion confirms customer commitment is deepening rather than retreating. Management's appointment of an AI-specialist CPO with Google Cloud and Oracle pedigree signals deliberate repositioning for the AI era.

All three threats are primarily acute for point-solution ITSM vendors rather than a multi-domain platform entrenched in Fortune 500 enterprises.
ai_disruption_view.net_assessment: Net positive over a 3-to-5-year horizon. Workflow orchestration complexity increases with AI agent proliferation. The more agents an enterprise deploys, the more it needs authoritative governance and coordination -- precisely what ServiceNow provides. Platform breadth across ITSM, HRSD, CSM, legal ops, security, and source-to-pay creates switching cost structures that AI-native point solutions cannot replicate quickly. Primary monitoring variable: whether Now Assist generates measurable ACV expansion per customer over the next 4-6 quarters. If it proves to be an upsell accelerant rather than a retention tool, confidence rises to 85+.
